title: Edward Bordeaux, the ragtime amateur who influenced him
summary: Hug names Edward Bordeaux, a non-professional who played rags from sheet music at the family home, as an early influence.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Were there any particular bands or specific musicians who were especially encouraging when you were just trying to get into the jazz or if you will ragtime playing?

Right. There were no specific musicians, Charlie, in the early period because if you will figure this, that I started taking lessons when I was about eight or nine years old. And, of course, that's pretty young, you know, especially when you go back into those old days and people, the way they were, you know, kind of strict, you didn't get much chance to get out too much. Right. I didn't meet too many musicians. I wasn't around too many musicians. But there was one man, his name was Edward Bordeaux. I have never mentioned this man's name prior to any other interviews, Charlie, and it's the first time that I have ever really gave this any real thought when you, you know, when you asked me did I ever meet any other musicians. And this man was really not a professional but played ragtime very fluently. And, you know, he used to come around the house and he couldn't play without the music. And he'd come with a rag, a roll of music, you know, wrapped up, you know, into his home and he'd sit there and he'd bring out these rags, you know, and he'd start playing chicken reel rag and, oh, good gravy rag. And I'd just go crazy to just listen to him play these rags. And he played them very, very mechanical and with not too much relaxation. But it was really one of the probably the oiliest influences that I had.
Would you remember how you spelled his name, Bordeaux, you said?
